faq.a: Cephalosporins cover Gram‑negative and some Gram‑positive bacteria; metronidazole adds anaerobic coverage typical of gut flora.
faq.q: Why give metronidazole with a cephalosporin?

faq.a: Only in selected stable patients with sealed perforation and no peritonitis; otherwise surgery is required.
faq.q: Can a perforated ulcer be managed non‑operatively?

faq.a: Rely on clinical signs (sudden severe pain, guarding, tachycardia) and proceed to exploratory laparotomy.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man with sudden epigastric pain and guarding – what is your immediate management? — Stabilize, give broad‑spectrum antibiotics, arrange urgent imaging or proceed to surgery if imaging unavailable.
How does free air on an upright X‑ray differentiate perforation from intestinal obstruction? — Free air indicates a breach of the GI wall; obstruction shows dilated loops without air under diaphragm.
Why is an omental patch preferred for a duodenal ulcer perforation? — Provides a vascular seal, is quick, and avoids extensive resection in a sick patient.

What are the key differences between perforated typhoid ileitis and perforated peptic ulcer? — Typhoid often presents with fever, multiple ileal perforations, and a history of prolonged fever; ulcer perforation is usually isolated, with a history of dyspepsia or NSAID use.
When would you choose laparoscopy over open laparotomy? — In hemodynamically stable patients with limited contamination and when equipment and expertise are available.
Why avoid aminoglycosides in a patient with suspected perforation and renal impairment? — They are nephrotoxic and can worsen renal failure in sepsis.
How does the presence of herbal remedy use affect your differential? — Certain herbs cause ulceration or vasculitis, increasing perforation risk; ask specifically in history.
ai.title: Enteric Perforation
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: A perforation of the gastrointestinal tract leads to peritonitis and sepsis. Prompt recognition, resuscitation and surgical repair are essential, especially in low‑resource settings where imaging may be limited.

b: Common causes: peptic ulcer disease, typhoid, tuberculosis, malaria‑related ischemia, trauma, NSAID use, herbal remedies
Typical presentation: sudden severe abdominal pain, guarding, fever, tachycardia
sections.p: Enteric perforation is a breach in the wall of the stomach, small intestine or colon that releases luminal contents into the peritoneal cavity, causing chemical and bacterial peritonitis.

b: Free intraperitoneal air on upright X‑ray = perforation
Ultrasound: reverberation artefact (air) and fluid collections
sections.p: Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, basic imaging and laboratory clues. In low‑resource hospitals, plain abdominal X‑ray and bedside ultrasound are often the only tools.

b: Broad‑spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole)
Urgent laparotomy or laparoscopy for closure
sections.p: Peritonitis rapidly progresses to septic shock; early resuscitation and source control (surgical repair) reduce mortality, which can exceed 30 % without timely intervention.

t.b: Detects free air under diaphragm; confirms perforation
Shows free fluid, air artefacts; useful when X‑ray unavailable

b: Empiric antibiotics: third‑generation cephalosporin + metronidazole; avoid aminoglycosides if renal dysfunction
Surgical options: primary closure with omental patch for duodenal ulcer, resection with anastomosis for ischemic bowel
If no imaging, proceed to exploratory laparotomy based on clinical signs
sections.p: Treat the cause, control infection, and support organ function. Surgical repair is definitive; choice of technique depends on site and patient stability.

b: Acute pancreatitis – pain radiates to back, serum amylase ↑, no free air
Acute appendicitis – localized RLQ tenderness, no pneumoperitoneum
Intestinal obstruction – distended loops, absent air under diaphragm
sections.p: Other acute abdomen causes can mimic perforation.

b: Normal X‑ray early in perforation; repeat after 6 h if suspicion persists
Leukocytosis may be absent in immunocompromised or malnourished patients
sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.

b: Guarding and rigidity are late signs; look for early peritoneal irritation (rebound tenderness)
In resource‑limited settings, a positive “air under diaphragm” on a single portable X‑ray is sufficient to operate
sections.p: Focus on bedside reasoning and emergency priorities.
